base_method_text.title:
Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model
  Scaling Laws
base_method_text.summary:
Large language model (LLM) scaling laws are empirical formulas that estimate
changes in model quality as a result of increasing parameter count and training
data. However, these formulas, including the popular Deepmind Chinchilla
scaling laws, neglect to include the cost of inference. We modify the
Chinchilla scaling laws to calculate the optimal LLM parameter count and
pre-training data size to train and deploy a model of a given quality and
inference demand. We conduct our analysis both in terms of a compute budget and
real-world costs and find that LLM researchers expecting reasonably large
inference demand (~1B requests) should train models smaller and longer than
Chinchilla-optimal. Furthermore, we train 47 models of varying sizes and
parameter counts to validate our formula and find that model quality continues
to improve as we scale tokens per parameter to extreme ranges (up to 10,000).
Finally, we ablate the procedure used to fit the Chinchilla scaling law
coefficients and find that developing scaling laws only from data collected at
typical token/parameter ratios overestimates the impact of additional tokens at
these extreme ranges.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper addresses the limitations of existing LLM scaling laws, such as the Chinchilla scaling laws, which do not account for inference costs. It modifies these laws to determine the optimal model size and training data size considering both training and inference demands. The study validates the modified scaling laws through extensive experiments and ablates the curve fitting procedure, revealing that existing laws overestimate the impact of additional training data in extreme data regimes.
base_method_text.methodology: The research modifies the Chinchilla scaling laws by incorporating inference costs into the optimization problem. It uses pre-training cross-entropy loss as a proxy for model quality and FLOPs as the unit of computational cost. The optimization problem is solved computationally using the Newton root-finding method. Real-world cost optimality is estimated by accounting for hardware utilization and costs.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The study involves training 47 models with the MPT architecture, ranging from 150M to 6B parameters, with data budgets from 10 to 10,000 tokens per parameter. The models are evaluated on a version of the open-source Evaluation Gauntlet, which includes tasks in world knowledge, commonsense reasoning, reading comprehension, language understanding, and symbolic problem-solving.
base_method_text.limitations: The analysis assumes that LLM practitioners can estimate inference demand prior to training. The experimental data is limited in terms of model size (up to 6B parameters) and the number of training runs (47 vs. 400 in the Chinchilla paper). The real-world cost estimation model simplifies hardware utilization and costs, leaving aside latency requirements and assuming MFU and cost per FLOP do not depend on model size, configuration, or sequence length.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring scaling laws beyond 10,000 tokens per parameter and at larger model sizes. Further work is needed to develop scaling laws that apply precisely at a wide range of ratios and to understand the limits of scaling law extrapolation. Additional research is also suggested to explore the minimum data required to accurately fit scaling laws coefficients.

add_method_texts.title: Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models
add_method_texts.summary:
Scaling laws are powerful tools to predict the performance of large language
models. However, current scaling laws fall short of accounting for inference
costs. In this work, we first show that model architecture affects inference
latency, where models of the same size can have up to 3.5x difference in
latency. To tackle this challenge, we modify the Chinchilla scaling laws to
co-optimize the model parameter count, the number of training tokens, and the
model architecture. Due to the reason that models of similar training loss
exhibit gaps in downstream evaluation, we also propose a novel method to train
inference-efficient models based on the revised scaling laws. We perform
extensive empirical studies to fit and evaluate our inference-aware scaling
laws. We vary model parameters from 80M to 1B, training tokens from 1.6B to
30B, and model shapes, training a total of 63 models. Guided by our
inference-efficient scaling law and model selection method, we release the
Morph-1B model, which improves inference latency by 1.8x while maintaining
accuracy on downstream tasks compared to open-source models, pushing the Pareto
frontier of accuracy-latency tradeoff.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper addresses the problem of inference costs being disregarded by current scaling laws for large language models (LLMs). It introduces inference-efficient scaling laws that co-optimize model parameter count, training tokens, and model architecture. A novel method is proposed to train inference-efficient models based on the revised scaling laws, and the Morph-1B model is released, demonstrating improved inference latency while maintaining accuracy.
add_method_texts.methodology: The research modifies the Chinchilla scaling laws to incorporate model architecture considerations. It involves training multiple models with varying parameters, tokens, and shapes, then fitting the inference-efficient scaling laws using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. A novel method is developed to rank model architectural choices based on loss predictions from scaling laws.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: Experiments involved training over 60 models ranging from 80M to 1B parameters and 1.6B to 30B tokens. Models were evaluated on 11 downstream tasks used by Open-LM, and inference latency was measured on a single NVIDIA Ampere 40GB A100 GPU. The DCLM-Baseline dataset was used for training, and zero-shot evaluation was performed using LLM-foundry.
add_method_texts.limitations: The training was not scaled to include 7B models due to resource limitations. The scaling laws are based on specific model architectures and may not generalize to all architectures. The study also acknowledges that recently developed inference systems could introduce new trade-offs.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include scaling training to larger models (e.g., 7B), exploring the impact of new inference systems and architectural optimizations (like MQA, GQA, MLA) on the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, and further refining the scaling laws to account for these factors. The work also calls for designing language models with inference efficiency as a primary consideration.

base_experimental_code:
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import Optional, Sequence, Union

import torch
from torch.optim import Optimizer

from composer.core import Algorithm, Event, State, Time, TimeUnit
from composer.loggers import Logger

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def apply_alibi(
    model: torch.nn.Module,
    max_sequence_length: int,
    optimizers: Optional[Union[Optimizer, Sequence[Optimizer]]] = None,
) -> None:
    """Removes position embeddings and replaces the attention function and attention mask
    as per :class:`.Alibi`. Note that the majority of the training speed-up from using ALiBi
    comes from being able to train on shorter sequence lengths; this function does not scale
    the training sequence length as :class:`.Alibi` does, so little speedup will be
    observed from using it alone. See the :doc:`Method Card </method_cards/alibi>` for
    more details. This function should be called after the model is instantiated and
    before training begins.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        import composer.functional as cf

        cf.apply_alibi(
            model=model,
            max_sequence_length=512
        )

    Args:
        model (torch.nn.Module): Model to transform.
        max_sequence_length (int): Maximum sequence length that the
            model will be able to accept. Internally, the transformations applied by alibi
            change sequence-shaped tensors to handle sequences up to ``max_sequence_length``.
            Depending on ``max_sequence_length`` and ``model`` these changes could increase
            or decrease the model's maximum sequence length.

            At minimum, ``max_sequence_length`` should be set to the sequence length used
            during training. However, if evaluating on sequence lengths longer than those
            used in training, ``max_sequence_length`` should be set accordingly.

            Note that larger ``max_sequence_length`` means a larger memory footprint of
            the model. So, it is best to set this parameter equal the longest
            sequence length that will be seen during training and/or evaluation.
        optimizers (torch.optim.Optimizer | Sequence[torch.optim.Optimizer], optional):
            Existing optimizers bound to ``model.parameters()``. All optimizers that have already been
            constructed with ``model.parameters()`` must be specified here so
            they will optimize the correct parameters.

            If the optimizer(s) are constructed *after* calling this function,
            then it is safe to omit this parameter. These optimizers will see the correct
            model parameters.
    """
    try:
        from composer.algorithms.alibi.attention_surgery_functions import policy_registry
    except ImportError as e:
        raise MissingConditionalImportError(extra_deps_group='nlp', conda_package='transformers') from e

    # To use model surgery utilities, we need to define a policy of type
    # Mapping[Type[torch.nn.Module], ReplacementFunction], where ReplacementFunction is
    # Callable[[torch.nn.Module, Optional[int]], Optional[torch.nn.Module]].
    #
    # This mapping is built by the source code in `attention_surgery_functions/`, but
    # needs to be completed here by "freezing" alibi-specific arguments.
    #
    # For additional details, see `attention_surgery_functions/utils.py`.
    def as_replacement_function(surgery_function):

        def replacement_function(module: torch.nn.Module, module_index: int):
            return surgery_function(module, module_index, max_sequence_length=max_sequence_length)

        return replacement_function

    # Wrap each alibi_surgery_function as a ReplacementFunction by "freezing" `max_sequence_length`
    policies = {
        module_class: as_replacement_function(alibi_surgery_function)
        for module_class, alibi_surgery_function in policy_registry.items()
    }

    # Note: `policies` defines replacements for _all_ the modules registered in `policy_registry`,
    # meaning that some replacements may be irrelevant for `model`.
    # Conversely, attention modules within `model` may be ignored if they are not registered by the
    # implementations within `./attention_surgery_functions/`.
    replaced_pairs = module_surgery.replace_module_classes(model, optimizers=optimizers, policies=policies)

    count = len(replaced_pairs)
    if count == 0:
        supported_modules = ''.join(sorted([f'\n\t{c.__module__}.{c.__name__}' for c in policy_registry.keys()]))
        log.warning(
            f'ALiBi had no effect on the model! Support for ALiBi surgery ' \
            f'is currently limited to the following classes: {supported_modules}')
    else:
        log.info(f'{count} instances of ALiBi added')
base_experimental_info:
- apply_alibi: Removes position embeddings and replaces the attention function and attention mask in a model to implement ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases).
- Supported module classes: Lists the classes for which ALiBi surgery is currently supported.
new_method:
Building on the Base Method’s cost-sensitive scaling laws and drawing from the Add Method’s focus on co-optimizing architecture for inference efficiency, the newly proposed method is a two-phase “Adaptive Architecture + Mixed-Precision” approach:

1) Phase One – Multi-Objective Architectural Search  
   • Instead of fixing the model architecture a priori (as in the Base Method), we introduce a joint search over parameter count, training token count, and architecture “shape.”  
   • Borrowing the Add Method’s insight that shape significantly affects latency—even at the same parameter count—we define shape descriptors (e.g., width/depth ratios, attention head configurations) and systematically explore them.  
   • We incorporate a multi-objective cost function that balances total training cost (FLOPs, wall-clock time) against per-token inference latency and memory overhead. Unlike existing methods that primarily fit a curve to total FLOPs, our approach models concurrency factors (e.g., batch size constraints, GPU memory limits) to reflect real-world throughput considerations.

2) Phase Two – Mixed-Precision Fine-Tuning  
   • After identifying an architecture from Phase One that lies on the Pareto frontier of training cost vs. inference cost, we fine-tune in mixed precision, dynamically switching between higher-precision formats (for layers sensitive to numerical stability) and lower-precision formats (for less sensitive layers).  
   • This goes beyond partial numeric precision tweaks by allowing selective precision assignments that can adapt during fine-tuning: if a particular layer’s gradient variance surpasses a threshold, we temporarily revert it to higher precision, mitigating quality degradation.  
   • Crucially, this phase ensures that any architecture that emerges from Phase One can be further optimized for inference speed without substantially harming downstream task accuracy.  

Why This Approach Is Novel:  
• It does not merely augment the Base Method’s formula with a single extra term; rather, it introduces a fully integrated search over architectural design, concurrency-aware inference cost, and dynamic precision assignment.  
• By systematically orchestrating architecture search, cost modeling, and per-layer precision adjustments, it addresses multiple overlooked practicalities—such as the often-changing latency profile under varied concurrency loads and the interplay between numeric stability and architectural shape.  
• Compared to the Add Method alone, which treats architecture co-optimization as largely fixed once chosen, the adaptive precision step extends inference efficiency gains while maintaining (and sometimes improving) predictive performance.  

Overall, this “Adaptive Architecture + Mixed-Precision” strategy directly tackles both the Base Method’s limited architectural variability and the unaccounted-for inference dynamics, offering a holistic approach to developing cost-aware and inference-optimized language models.
